audience: Complete beginner. One concept per lesson. Tasks under 20 minutes. Less reading, more visuals and hands-on work.

aligned_with.lesson_ids: Same ids as LESSON_ORDER. L10–L12 are previews in the app today; this file supplies their full workbook content.
aligned_with.notes: Student-facing wording matches the current app. expected_stdout is print() output only (the app stores prompts on r.prompts, not r.out). Strip # comments before applying rule patterns, as ruleChecks already does.

skills_map.name: Python fundamentals
skills_map.later: Kept sharp in every later phase, especially Python foundations.
skills_map.why: Every AI tool you use later is written in Python, or called from it.

skills_map.name: Data handling
skills_map.later: Seeing data (~6 weeks): tables, files, cleaning, and a dashboard.
skills_map.why: Lists and dictionaries are how programs hold rows and records. Later you will load real datasets.

skills_map.name: ML basics
skills_map.later: Classical ML (~10 weeks): train/test split, a first model, and reading its score.
skills_map.why: Job posts expect you to train a simple model and explain what the score means.

skills_map.name: LLM APIs
skills_map.later: Neural nets, then LLMs (~16 weeks): call a model, send a prompt, read the reply.
skills_map.why: AI engineer work is mostly talking to models through an API, not training one from scratch.

skills_map.name: Prompt engineering
skills_map.later: Neural nets, then LLMs: write, test, and tighten prompts on purpose.
skills_map.why: L4 already shows that the exact wording of a prompt (even a trailing space) changes what you get back.

skills_map.name: RAG
skills_map.later: Building AI apps (~16 weeks): retrieve from your own documents, then generate an answer.
skills_map.why: Most production AI apps answer from a company's files, not from the model's memory alone.

skills_map.name: Agents / tool use
skills_map.later: Building AI apps capstone: an agent that calls tools and a RAG pipeline.
skills_map.why: A function is a tool you can call. A chat loop that picks a path (help, name, bye) is the same idea as an agent choosing a tool.

skills_map.name: Evaluation
skills_map.later: Classical ML and Building AI apps: test sets, rubrics, and checking model answers.
skills_map.why: Check uses exact matches and ordered rules, the same habit you need when you score a model.

skills_map.name: Deployment / MLOps
skills_map.later: Building AI apps: put a working app on the web, log runs, and watch it break safely.
skills_map.why: A project is not done until someone else can open it and use it.

skills_map.name: Safety
skills_map.later: Building AI apps: prompt injection, secrets, and what the app must refuse.
skills_map.why: Exact-match checks, a clear quit path, and not treating every input as trusted start here.

milestones.title: Mini chat program
milestones.description: A tiny chatbot that greets you by name, answers a few commands, and quits on bye. This is Lesson 12, cleaned up for a public repo.
checklist: Public GitHub repo with a short README: what it does, how to run it, a sample conversation.
One screenshot or copy-pasted chat transcript in the README.
The program greets by name, handles help / name / bye, and never loops forever.
Code is a single .py file a reviewer can run with `python3 chat.py`.

milestones.title: Small game
milestones.description: A short text game (guess-the-number or a tiny adventure) that uses functions, loops, and data. Playable in the terminal, with win and lose paths.
checklist: README with how to play, the rules, and one sample run.
Replayable: you can start a new game without restarting the file by hand.
At least two functions (for example, start_game and check_guess).
No infinite loop; there is a quit command or a turn limit.

milestones.title: Data dashboard
milestones.description: Load a real CSV, clean a few messy values, and show 2–3 charts that answer a question. A notebook or small web page is fine.
checklist: README states the question, the data source, and how to run it.
The data file (or a download script) lives with the project.
Charts have titles and axis labels a stranger can read.
A short 'what I found' section with one honest limitation.

milestones.title: Visual explorer
milestones.description: An interactive picture of one idea you need for ML, such as a line fit or a loss curve. Sliders or simple inputs change the picture.
checklist: README explains the picture in plain words, then the math in one short block.
A screenshot of the default view and one 'what happens if I change X' note.
The visual updates when you change a value.
No formula appears without a picture next to it.

milestones.title: Trained model
milestones.description: Train a classic model on a public dataset, report a test score, and show two mistakes it made. Keep the pipeline reproducible.
checklist: README: problem, data, model type, test score, and how to rerun from scratch.
A train/test split, with the test score coming only from the test set.
Saved metrics (and the model or a seed) so a reviewer gets the same number.
A short error analysis: two examples it got wrong, and a guess why.

milestones.title: LLM app or notebook
milestones.description: A small app that calls an LLM API with a clear prompt, shows the reply, and compares two prompt versions. No training required.
checklist: README: what the app does, which API, and how to set a key without committing it.
A .env.example (no real secrets) and the key loaded from the environment.
Two saved prompt versions and a short note on which was better, and why.
A refusal or guard for one unsafe or off-topic request.

milestones.title: RAG or agent capstone
milestones.description: A deployed AI app that answers from your documents (RAG) or calls tools (agent). This is the portfolio centerpiece.
checklist: Live link plus source repo. README has a 60-second demo (gif or video).
A documented architecture: retrieve or tool call, then generate.
At least five evaluation examples, including one failure.
Secrets stay out of git. Basic safety: off-topic and injection cases are handled.
A 'how to run locally' section that actually works on a clean machine.

l1.title: Print and Hello
l1.concept: `print` is how you put words on the screen. That's the whole lesson.

see.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["You type
print(\"Hello\")"] --> B[Python runs it] B --> C["The screen shows
Hello"]
see.explain: You write one print line. Python runs it and shows whatever was inside the quotes.

predict.why: print shows the text inside the quotes, not the quotes themselves.

options: Hi then Cole, on two lines
predict.why: Each print starts a new line.

prompts.change: Change the text inside the quotes from Hello to Hi, then run it.
prompts.expect: The screen shows Hi.

prompts.change: Add a second line: print("Cole"), then run it.
prompts.expect: Two lines appear: Hi (or Hello) on the first line, Cole on the second.

fix.bug: Hello is not in quotes, so Python looks for a variable named Hello.
fix.hint: If you want the word itself, wrap it in quotes.

build.task: Write one line that prints Hello. Run it. You should see Hello.

rules.pass_text: You used `print()`
rules.fail_text: This needs a `print()` line
rules.correction: Add a line that starts with `print(`.
rules.hint: The whole lesson is one line: `print("Hello")`.

rules.pass_text: You're printing Hello
rules.fail_text: The lesson asks you to print Hello
rules.correction: Put Hello inside the quotes.
rules.hint: Whatever is inside the quotes is what appears on the screen.

tests.pass_text: Running it prints Hello
tests.fail_text: Running it doesn't print Hello yet
tests.correction: Check the spelling inside the quotes.
tests.hint: Whatever is inside the quotes is what appears on the screen.

l2.title: Strings vs variables
l2.concept: Quotes make a string: Python prints exactly what's inside. A name without quotes is a variable: Python looks up what you stored there.

see.mermaid:
flowchart LR A["print(\"name\")
quotes around the word"] --> B["shows the word
name"] C["print(name)
no quotes, a variable"] --> D["shows the value
Cole Jackson"]
see.explain: Quotes mean print this exact text. No quotes means look up the variable and print what is stored there.

predict.why: Quotes make a string, so Python prints the word name.
No quotes, so Python looks up the variable and prints Cole.

prompts.change: Change the stored text from Cole to Jackson, then run it.
prompts.expect: The screen shows Jackson.

prompts.change: Change print(name) to print("name"), then run it.
prompts.expect: The screen shows the word name, not Jackson.

fix.bug: Quotes around the variable name print the word, not the stored value.
fix.hint: Use the variable's name with no quotes when you want the value.

build.task: Store your name in a variable, then print the variable and print `"name"`. Notice the difference.
build.starter: # Lesson 2: store your name, then print it two ways

rules.pass_text: You stored text in a variable
rules.fail_text: Store your name in a variable first
rules.correction: Write something like `name = "Cole Jackson"`.
rules.hint: The quotes go around the text you store, not around the variable's name.

rules.pass_text: You printed the variable, not the word
rules.fail_text: Print the variable without quotes around its name
rules.correction: Use `print(name)`, not `print("name")`, to see the stored value.
rules.hint: Quotes tell Python to print the exact text inside them.

rules.pass_text: You also printed the word name, for comparison
rules.fail_text: Optional: also print `"name"` to compare
rules.correction: This one is extra. `print("name")` shows the word name.
rules.hint: One has quotes, one doesn't. That's the whole point of this lesson.

tests.pass_text: Running it shows the value you stored
tests.fail_text: Running it doesn't show your stored value
tests.correction: Only the word name (or nothing) showed up. Print the variable itself.
tests.hint: `print(name)` with no quotes.

l3.title: Numbers and math
l3.concept: Numbers do math. Strings join. Same `+` sign, two different jobs. Other math operators: `-` subtract, `*` multiply, `/` divide.

see.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["5 + 3
two numbers"] -->|adds| B["8
math"] C["'5' + '3'
two strings"] -->|joins| D["53
concatenation"]
see.explain: With no quotes, + adds. With quotes, + glues text together — that joining is called concatenation.

predict.why: No quotes, so + does math.
Both are strings, so they join. That's concatenation, not math.

prompts.change: Change 5 + 3 to 5 * 3, then run it.
prompts.expect: The first line shows 15. * multiplies.

prompts.change: Change "5" + "3" to "5" + "30", then run it.
prompts.expect: The second line shows 530. The strings join, they do not add.

fix.bug: You cannot join a string and a number with +.
fix.hint: Make both sides the same type: two numbers for math, or two strings to join.

build.task: Print a number addition (like 5 + 3) and a string join (like "5" + "3"). Predict both results before you run them.

rules.pass_text: You added two numbers
rules.fail_text: Add two numbers with no quotes
rules.correction: Try `print(5 + 3)` and you should see 8.
rules.hint: Numbers have no quotes around them.

rules.pass_text: You joined two strings
rules.fail_text: Join two quoted pieces of text with `+`
rules.correction: Try `print("5" + "3")` and you should see 53.
rules.hint: Same `+` sign, different job, because the types are different.

tests.pass_text: Running it shows 8 (math)
tests.fail_text: Running it doesn't show 8
tests.correction: Add a line like `print(5 + 3)`.
tests.hint: No quotes around numbers you want to add.

tests.pass_text: Running it shows 53 (joined strings)
tests.fail_text: Running it doesn't show 53
tests.correction: Add a line like `print("5" + "3")`.
tests.hint: Quotes turn numbers into text.

l4.title: input() and joining
l4.concept: `input()` asks a question and waits. The answer is a string. You can join strings with `+`.

see.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["input(\"food\")
no space at the end"] --> B["foodChicken
the answer sticks"] C["input(\"food \")
space inside the quotes"] --> D["food Chicken
a readable line"]
see.explain: input() prints the prompt exactly as written, then waits. Put a space before the closing quote so the answer does not stick to the question.

predict.why: + joins the sentence and the value. The space lives inside the quotes.
There is no space inside either string, so the words stick together.

tweak.starter:
food = input("What's your favorite food? ")
print("You like " + food)

prompts.change: Delete the space just before the closing quote in the input prompt, run it, and type Chicken.
prompts.expect: The question and the answer stick: foodChicken. Put the space back.

prompts.change: Keep the prompt space, but change "You like " to "You like" (no space), then type tacos.
prompts.expect: The sentence becomes You liketacos. The space has to live inside the quotes.

fix.bug: The prompt is missing a space at the end, so the answer sticks: foodChicken.
fix.broken:
food = input("What's your favorite food?")
print("You like " + food)
fix.hint: The space has to live inside the quotes, right before the closing quote.
fix.fixed:
food = input("What's your favorite food? ")
print("You like " + food)

build.task: Ask for a food with input() and print a sentence that includes the answer. Check that the sentence looks right.
build.starter: # Lesson 4: ask for a food, then print a sentence
build.reference:
food = input("What's your favorite food? ")
print("You like " + food)

rules.pass_text: You used `input()` to ask a question
rules.fail_text: This needs an `input()` line
rules.correction: Ask the question with `input("What's your favorite food? ")`.
rules.hint: The answer comes back as a string, ready to join into a sentence.

rules.pass_text: The prompt has a space at the end
rules.fail_text: The prompt is missing a space at the end
rules.correction: Put a space before the closing quote, like `input("What's your favorite food? ")`.
rules.hint: Without that space, you get something like foodChicken.

rules.pass_text: You joined the answer into a sentence
rules.fail_text: Join the answer onto some text with `+`
rules.correction: Try `print("You like " + food)`.
rules.hint: Leave a space inside the quoted text so the sentence reads naturally.

tests.pass_text: Answering Chicken prints a sentence with Chicken
tests.fail_text: Answering Chicken didn't print it back
tests.correction: We typed Chicken, but it never appeared in the output. Print the variable you stored the answer in.
tests.hint: Like `print("You like " + food)`.

l5.title: int() and str()
l5.concept: `input()` always gives you text. `int()` turns text into a number so you can do math. `str()` turns a number into text so you can join it into a sentence.

see.mermaid:
flowchart LR A[\"'15'\"
text from input()] -->|int()| B["15
after int()"] B -->|+ 1| C["16
after adding 1"] C -->|str()| D[\"'16'\"
after str()]
see.explain: input() gives you text like '15', and int() makes it a number so you can add 1. str() turns 16 back into text so you can join it into a sentence.

predict.why: You cannot join a string and a number with +. Read the TypeError from the bottom.
int() turns the text 15 into a number, so + 1 is math.

tweak.starter:
age = int(input("How old are you? "))
print("Next year you'll be " + str(age + 1))

prompts.change: Run it and type 15.
prompts.expect: The sentence includes 16.

prompts.change: Remove str() so the print joins the sentence with age + 1 directly, then type 15.
prompts.expect: TypeError. Read it from the bottom: it tells you about str and int. Then put str() back.

fix.bug: Joining a string and a number with + causes a TypeError.
fix.hint: Read the error from the bottom. The last line names the problem. Wrap the number in str().

build.task: Ask for a number, add one, and print a sentence that includes the new number.
build.starter: # Lesson 5: ask for a number, add one, print a sentence
build.reference:
age = int(input("How old are you? "))
print("Next year you'll be " + str(age + 1))

rules.pass_text: You used `int()` to make a number
rules.fail_text: This needs `int()` to turn text into a number
rules.correction: Wrap the answer, like `age = int(input("How old are you? "))`.
rules.hint: If you add text to a number, Python shows a TypeError. Read that error from the bottom.

rules.pass_text: You used `str()` when joining a number into a sentence
rules.fail_text: Use `str()` when you join a number onto text
rules.correction: Write something like `print("Next year you'll be " + str(age + 1))`.
rules.hint: `"Total: " + 15` fails. `"Total: " + str(15)` works.

tests.pass_text: Answering 15 prints a sentence with 16
tests.fail_text: Answering 15 didn't show 16
tests.correction: We typed 15 and expected to see 16 in the output.
tests.hint: int() the answer, add 1, then str() it to join.

l6.title: if/else and ==
l6.concept: `if` and `else` let the program choose a path. `==` means is exactly this.

see.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A[Ask for the password] --> B{"password == \"python\"?"}
    B -->|yes| C[Access granted]
    B -->|no| D[Access denied]
see.explain: The program asks one yes/no question, and == checks for an exact match. else is the path for every other answer.

predict.why: == is true when the value is exactly python, so it takes the if path.
>= compares strings A-to-Z. zebra comes after python, so this is true. Use == for a password.

prompts.change: Run it and type python, then run it again and type zebra.
prompts.expect: python prints Access granted. zebra prints Access denied.

prompts.change: Change == to >=, then type zebra.
prompts.expect: zebra gets in, because zebra comes after python in the alphabet. Change it back to ==.

fix.bug: >= is not a match check. With >=, zebra got through because zebra comes after python in the alphabet.
fix.hint: Use == when you want an exact match, not >=.

build.task: Ask for a password. If it is exactly `python`, print Access granted. Otherwise print Access denied. Try the right password and a wrong one.
build.starter: # Lesson 6: check the password with if/else

rules.pass_text: You used `if` to make a choice
rules.fail_text: This needs an `if` line
rules.correction: Start with `if password == "python":`.
rules.hint: The line after `if` has to be indented.

rules.pass_text: You're checking with `==`
rules.fail_text: `>=` is being used on a password or a string
rules.correction: Swap `>=` for `==`. `>=` let zebra through because zebra comes after python in the alphabet.
rules.hint: `>=` is for greater-or-equal, not for matching a password.

rules.pass_text: You're checking with `==`
rules.fail_text: Use `==` for an exact match
rules.correction: Write `if password == "python":`.
rules.hint: `==` means is this exactly that.

rules.pass_text: You have an `else` path too
rules.fail_text: Add an `else` for the wrong password
rules.correction: After the `if` block, add `else:` and print Access denied.
rules.hint: `else` runs only when the `if` check is false.

tests.pass_text: The password python gets in
tests.fail_text: The password python didn't get in
tests.correction: We typed python but didn't see Access granted.
tests.hint: Use `if password == "python":`.

tests.pass_text: The password zebra is blocked
tests.fail_text: The password zebra got in
tests.correction: We typed zebra and saw Access granted. That's the `>=` bug: zebra comes after python in the alphabet.
tests.hint: Use `==` for an exact match.

l7.title: elif and order
l7.concept: `elif` adds more paths. Python checks from the top and stops at the first true condition. Order matters.

see.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A{"score >= 90?"} -->|yes| GA[A]
    A -->|no| B{"score >= 80?"}
    B -->|yes| GB[B]
    B -->|no| C{"score >= 70?"}
    C -->|yes| GC[C]
    C -->|no| E[else] --> GF[F]
see.caption: Python stops at the first "yes".
see.explain: Python starts at the top of the ladder and stops at the first true check. Put the highest score check first.

predict.why: 95 is >= 90, so it stops at the first check and prints A.
Python stops at the first true condition. 95 is also >= 70, so it never reaches the A check.

prompts.change: Run it with score = 95, then change score to 80 and run again.
prompts.expect: 95 prints A. 80 prints B.

prompts.change: Put the >= 70 check first, then run it with score = 95.
prompts.expect: It prints C, because 95 is also >= 70 and Python never reaches A. Put >= 90 back first.

fix.bug: If you check >= 70 first, 95 gets a C, because 95 is also >= 70 and Python never reaches the A check.
fix.hint: Put the highest threshold first. Python stops at the first true condition.

build.task: Ask for a score with int(input()). Print A for 90+, B for 80+, C for 70+, and F otherwise. Put the highest check first. Leave the right order in the editor when you hit Check.
build.starter: # Lesson 7: grades with if / elif / else

rules.pass_text: You used `elif` for more than two paths
rules.fail_text: This needs at least one `elif`
rules.correction: After your `if`, add `elif score >= 80:` and so on.
rules.hint: Python checks from the top and stops at the first true condition.

rules.pass_text: The highest score check comes first
rules.fail_text: The conditions are in the wrong order
rules.correction: Put the highest threshold first, like `>= 90`, then `>= 80`, then `>= 70`.
rules.hint: If `>= 70` comes first, 95 is true right away and gets a C.

tests.pass_text: A score of 95 gets an A
tests.fail_text: A score of 95 doesn't get an A
tests.correction: Put `>= 90` first.
tests.hint: Python stops at the first true condition.

tests.pass_text: A score of 80 gets a B
tests.fail_text: A score of 80 doesn't get a B
tests.correction: After `>= 90`, check `>= 80` for a B.
tests.hint: 80 is not >= 90, but it is >= 80.

tests.pass_text: A score of 70 gets a C
tests.fail_text: A score of 70 doesn't get a C
tests.correction: After the B check, use `>= 70` for a C.
tests.hint: Order is 90, then 80, then 70.

tests.pass_text: A score of 50 gets an F
tests.fail_text: A score of 50 doesn't get an F
tests.correction: Add an `else:` that prints F.
tests.hint: else runs when none of the score checks are true.

l8.title: while loops
l8.concept: A while loop repeats as long as a check is true. It needs three parts: SETUP, CHECK, and CHANGE.

see.animation: Draw SETUP once at the top: password = "". Arrow down to a diamond CHECK: password != "python"? If yes, still wrong, go to CHANGE: ask again with input(). Then a looping arrow labeled check again goes back to CHECK. If no, it matches, leave the circle to Access granted. A small caption under the exit: after the loop (optional print).
see.mermaid:
flowchart TD S["SETUP
password = \"\""] --> C{"CHECK
password != \"python\"?"} C -->|yes, still wrong| CH["CHANGE
ask again with input()"] CH -->|check again| C C -->|no, it matches| D[Access granted]
see.explain: SETUP gives the variable a starting value, and CHECK is the yes/no question. CHANGE updates the variable inside the loop so the check can eventually become false.

predict.code:
n = 1
while n < 3:
    print(n)
    n = n + 1
predict.why: When n becomes 3, the CHECK n < 3 is false, so the loop stops.
n never changes, so the CHECK stays true. Hit Stop, then add CHANGE inside the loop.

tweak.starter:
password = ""
while password != "python":
    password = input("What's the password? ")
print("Access granted")

prompts.change: Delete the input() line inside the loop, then run it.
prompts.expect: It loops forever because CHANGE is missing. Hit Stop, then put input() back inside the loop.

prompts.change: Change the first line to password = "python", then run it.
prompts.expect: The loop body never runs, because CHECK is already false. If you have a print after the loop, that print still runs. A final print is optional unless the task asks for one.

fix.bug: CHANGE is missing: input() is not inside the loop, so the password never updates and the loop never ends.
fix.broken:
password = ""
while password != "python":
    print("Wrong, try again")
print("Access granted")
fix.hint: Put input() inside the loop, indented under while, and store the answer in the same variable the CHECK uses.
fix.fixed:
password = ""
while password != "python":
    password = input("What's the password? ")
print("Access granted")

fix.bug: A student added stray spaces inside the quotes, and also thought a final print is required for the loop to work.
fix.broken:
password = ""
while password != "python":
    password = input("What's the password? ")
print(" Access granted ")
fix.hint: The loop is done when CHECK is false. A print after the loop is optional. If you do print something, the text inside the quotes is shown as written, so drop the extra spaces.
fix.fixed:
password = ""
while password != "python":
    password = input("What's the password? ")
print("Access granted")
fix.note: A final print is not required for a while loop to work. This task just happens to ask for one.

build.task: Write a while loop that keeps asking for the password until the answer is python. Use SETUP, CHECK, and CHANGE. A print after the loop is optional here.
build.reference:
password = ""
while password != "python":
    password = input("What's the password? ")
print("Access granted")

rules.pass_text: SETUP: the variable has a value before the loop
rules.fail_text: SETUP is missing: give the variable a starting value
rules.correction: A starting value like `password = ""` lets the CHECK run the first time.
rules.hint: If the variable doesn't exist yet, the CHECK has nothing to look at.

rules.pass_text: CHECK: you have a `while` line
rules.fail_text: CHECK is missing: this needs a `while` loop
rules.correction: Write `while password != "python":` and indent the next line.
rules.hint: The loop body keeps running as long as that check is true.

rules.pass_text: CHANGE: `input()` is inside the loop
rules.fail_text: CHANGE is missing: `input()` is not inside the loop
rules.correction: Put `password = input("What's the password? ")` inside the loop, indented under `while`.
rules.hint: If the password never changes inside the loop, you get an infinite loop. Hit the Stop button if that happens.

rules.pass_text: `Access granted` has no extra spaces
rules.fail_text: `Access granted` has extra spaces inside the quotes
rules.correction: Remove the stray spaces so it prints exactly `Access granted`.
rules.hint: A print after the loop is optional, but if you add one, the text inside the quotes is shown as written.

tests.pass_text: The loop stops right after python
tests.fail_text: The loop didn't stop at the right time
tests.correction: We typed hello, zebra, python. It should ask 3 times and stop.
tests.hint: input() goes inside the loop, and the CHECK compares to "python".

fail_if_out_of_inputs.fail_text: The loop kept asking after we typed python
fail_if_out_of_inputs.correction: We answered hello, zebra, then python, but it asked again. The CHECK never became false.
fail_if_out_of_inputs.hint: Make sure the CHECK compares the same variable that input() updates, like `while password != "python":`.

warmup.title: Password loop
warmup.concept: This is a short refresher after the break, not a new idea. Same three-part while loop you already know.

see.animation: Same three-part loop picture as Lesson 8, with these exact labels: SETUP password = ""; CHECK until the answer is python; CHANGE input("What's the password? "); yes arrow keep asking; no arrow got it; exit Access granted.
see.mermaid:
flowchart TD S["SETUP
password = \"\""] --> C{"CHECK
until the answer is python"} C -->|keep asking| CH["CHANGE
input(\"What's the password? \")"] CH --> C C -->|got it| D[Access granted]
see.explain: SETUP before the loop, CHECK at the top, CHANGE inside. That's the pattern that keeps you out of an infinite loop.

predict.code:
password = "python"

l9.title: Lists and for loops
l9.concept: A list is a row of items in brackets. The first item is index 0, not 1. `len()` counts the items. A for loop walks through each item, one at a time.

see.svg: A 340px-wide row of three boxes under the caption foods = [ … ] len(foods) is 3. Box 0: chicken, label foods[0]. Box 1: tacos, label foods[1]. Box 2: pizza, label foods[2]. Arrows from the boxes down to one terminal: for food in foods: print("I like " + food). Caption: one pass per item: chicken, then tacos, then pizza.
see.mermaid:
flowchart TD L["foods = [ … ] len(foods) is 3"] L --> I0["foods[0]
chicken"] L --> I1["foods[1]
tacos"] L --> I2["foods[2]
pizza"] I0 --> F["for food in foods:
print(\"I like \" + food)"] I1 --> F I2 --> F
labels: one pass per item: chicken, then tacos, then pizza
see.explain: The first box is foods[0], not foods[1]. A for loop takes each item in order, calls it food, and runs the indented lines once per item.

predict.why: Counting starts at 0, so foods[0] is the first item.
len counts the items (3). foods[1] is the second item.

prompts.change: Change foods[0] to foods[1], then run it.
prompts.expect: It prints tacos, not chicken. foods[1] is the second item.

prompts.change: Add "burgers" and "sushi" to the list, then print len(foods) again.
prompts.expect: len(foods) is 5. The last index is 4, not 5.

fix.bug: foods[1] was used as if it were the first item. Counting starts at 0.
fix.hint: The first item is foods[0]. foods[1] is the second item.

fix.bug: The running total never starts at 0, and nothing is added inside the loop.
fix.broken:
numbers = [3, 5, 7]
total = 0
for number in numbers:
    print(number)
print(total)
fix.hint: SETUP the total at 0, then CHANGE it each pass with total = total + number.
fix.fixed:
numbers = [3, 5, 7]
total = 0
for number in numbers:
    total = total + number
print(total)

build.task: Keep the three starter foods and add two more. Print foods[0] and len(foods). Then make numbers = [3, 5, 7], start with total = 0, add each number with a for loop, and print the total.
build.starter:

build.reference:

print(foods[0])
print(len(foods))
for food in foods:
    print("I like " + food)
numbers = [3, 5, 7]
total = 0
for number in numbers:
    total = total + number
print(total)

rules.fail_text: Make a list in square brackets `[]`

rules.hint: With 5 foods, len(foods) is 5, but the last index is 4.

l10.title: Functions
l10.concept: A function is a named recipe. You write it once with `def`, then call it whenever you need those steps.

see.mermaid:
flowchart TD A["You call
greet(\"Cole\")"] -->|jumps to the recipe| B["def greet(name):
name is Cole inside"] B -->|runs the body| C["The screen shows
Hello, Cole"]
see.explain: The name in parentheses is a parameter, a blank the caller fills in. When you write greet("Cole"), that blank is Cole for this one call.

predict.why: The function uses the value you passed in, which is Cole.

predict.code:
def add_one(n):
    return n + 1

print(add_one(5))
print(add_one(5) + 1)
predict.why: add_one(5) gives back 6. Then 6 + 1 is 7. return sends a value back to the caller.

prompts.change: Change greet("Cole") to greet("Maya"), then run it.
prompts.expect: It prints Hello, Maya.

prompts.change: Add a second call, greet("Cole"), under the first one.
prompts.expect: Two lines appear, one for each call. The recipe is reused.

fix.bug: The function is defined but never called, so nothing prints.
fix.hint: A def line only writes the recipe. You still have to call it, like greet("Cole").

fix.bug: The call happens before the def, so Python does not know greet yet.
fix.hint: Define the function first, then call it.

build.task: Write a function greet(name) that prints "Hello, " + name. Call it with "Cole". Then ask for a name with input() and call greet with that answer.
build.reference:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello, " + name)

greet("Cole")
person = input("What's your name? ")
greet(person)

rules.pass_text: You defined a function named `greet`
rules.fail_text: Define a function with `def greet(name):`
rules.correction: Start with `def greet(name):` and indent `print("Hello, " + name)`.
rules.hint: The def line names the recipe and its blank (the parameter).

rules.pass_text: You called `greet` (the def line plus at least one call)
rules.fail_text: Call `greet` after you define it
rules.correction: After the function, write `greet("Cole")`. Then ask for a name and call it again.
rules.hint: Defining a function does not run it. The call is what runs it.

rules.pass_text: You asked for a name with `input()`
rules.fail_text: Ask for a name and pass it to `greet`
rules.correction: Use `person = input("What's your name? ")` then `greet(person)`.
rules.hint: The answer is a string, which greet already knows how to use.

rules.pass_text: The greeting includes `Hello, ` with a space
rules.fail_text: Print `Hello, ` plus the name
rules.correction: Inside the function, `print("Hello, " + name)` keeps a space after the comma.
rules.hint: The space has to live inside the quotes, same idea as Lesson 4.

tests.pass_text: It greets Cole, then greets the name we typed (Maya)
tests.fail_text: It didn't print both Hello, Cole and Hello, Maya
tests.correction: Call `greet("Cole")`, then ask for a name and call `greet` with the answer. We typed Maya.
tests.hint: The function should run twice: once with Cole, once with the input.

l11.title: Dictionaries
l11.concept: A dictionary is a labeled box, not a numbered row. You look things up by the label (the key), not by a position number.

see.svg: A card titled person with two labeled rows: name → Cole, city → Austin. An arrow from person["city"] to Austin. A second, faded arrow from person[0] to a KeyError box, to show list-style indexes do not work here.
see.mermaid:
flowchart LR P["person
name → Cole
city → Austin"] -->|person['city']| V[Austin] P -->|person[0]| E[KeyError]
see.explain: The key is the label on the left, so person["city"] means give me the value for city. There is no person[0] unless you actually made a key named 0.

predict.why: You look up a dictionary by its label. The city label stores Austin.
person["city"] = "Dallas" updates that label. The next lookup sees the new value.

prompts.change: Change the lookup from person["city"] to person["name"], then run it.
prompts.expect: It prints Cole.

prompts.change: Add person["city"] = "Dallas" and print person["city"] again.
prompts.expect: It prints Dallas. The label now points at the new value.

fix.bug: A dictionary is not a list. person[0] looks for a key named 0, and that key is not there.
fix.hint: Use the label, like person["name"] or person["city"].

fix.bug: Keys are case-sensitive. "City" is not the same label as "city".
fix.hint: Match the key exactly, including lowercase.

build.task: Make a dictionary named person with name "Cole", city "Austin", and food "pizza". Print person["city"]. Ask for a new food, store it in person["food"], then print person["food"].
build.reference:
person = {"name": "Cole", "city": "Austin", "food": "pizza"}
print(person["city"])
person["food"] = input("New food: ")
print(person["food"])

rules.pass_text: You made a dictionary with `{` `}` and keys
rules.fail_text: Make a dictionary in curly braces, with keys and values
rules.correction: Write `person = {"name": "Cole", "city": "Austin", "food": "pizza"}`.
rules.hint: A dictionary uses labels, like "city": "Austin".

rules.pass_text: You looked up `person["city"]`
rules.fail_text: Print `person["city"]`
rules.correction: Add `print(person["city"])`.
rules.hint: The key goes inside quotes, inside the square brackets.

rules.pass_text: You updated `person["food"]`
rules.fail_text: Store the new food in `person["food"]`
rules.correction: Use `person["food"] = input("New food: ")`.
rules.hint: The same lookup syntax on the left side updates the value.

rules.pass_text: You asked for the new food with `input()`
rules.fail_text: Ask for a new food with `input()`
rules.correction: Put a space at the end of the prompt, like `input("New food: ")`.
rules.hint: input() always gives you a string, which is what a dictionary value can store.

tests.pass_text: It prints Austin, then the new food we typed (tacos)
tests.fail_text: It didn't print both Austin and tacos
tests.correction: Print person["city"] first. Then ask for a food, save it on person["food"], and print that.
tests.hint: We typed tacos as the new food.

l12.title: Mini chat
l12.concept: This is the Phase 0 finish line: a tiny chat program. You'll put input(), if/elif, and a while loop together so the program keeps talking until you say bye.

see.animation: First, a SETUP box: ask What's your name? and print Hi <name>! Type bye to quit. Then the familiar while-loop circle. CHECK: msg != "bye"? If yes, CHANGE with msg = input("You: "), then a small branch: help → I know: help, name, bye; name → You are <name>; else → I heard: <msg>. Arrow back to CHECK, labeled ask again. If CHECK is no (got bye), exit to Bye <name>!.
see.mermaid:
flowchart TD N["SETUP
ask name, greet, msg = \"\""] --> C{"CHECK
msg != \"bye\"?"} C -->|pick a reply| I["CHANGE
msg = input(\"You: \")"] I --> H{"if / elif / else"} H -->|help| R1[I know: help, name, bye] H -->|name| R2[You are name] H -->|other| R3[I heard: msg] H -->|bye| D[Bye name!] R1 -->|ask again| C R2 --> C R3 --> C C -->|got bye| D
see.explain: The loop keeps asking until the message is exactly bye, and if/elif picks one reply each pass. That is the same shape as an agent choosing a tool.

predict.why: elif checks the next path. help matches the second check, so it never reaches else.

predict.code:
msg = "bye"
while msg != "bye":
    print("still going")
print("done")
predict.why: CHECK is false right away, so the loop body never runs. Then the print after the loop runs.

prompts.change: Add an elif for "food" that prints I like pizza, then type food before bye.
prompts.expect: The food command takes that new path. Other commands still work.

prompts.change: Change the loop so it stops on quit instead of bye, then type bye, then quit.
prompts.expect: bye is treated like any other message (I heard: bye). Only quit ends the loop. Change it back to bye before you hit Check.

fix.bug: The chat asks for a first message outside the loop and never asks again, so it cannot reach bye unless that first answer already was bye.
fix.hint: Put input() inside the loop so every pass can get a new message, including bye.

fix.bug: A broad else-if is in the wrong order, or bye is checked with the wrong comparison, so the quit path never runs cleanly.
fix.hint: Handle bye inside the loop (or break on bye) so the program prints Bye <name>! and stops. Don't leave bye to the else path.

build.task: Build the mini chat. Ask "What's your name? " and print Hi <name>! Type bye to quit. Then loop with input("You: ") until the message is exactly bye. Commands: help prints I know: help, name, bye; name prints You are <name>; bye prints Bye <name>!; anything else prints I heard: <msg>.

rules.pass_text: You used `input()` to ask questions
rules.fail_text: This needs `input()` for the name and for each message
rules.correction: Ask `input("What's your name? ")`, then `input("You: ")` inside the loop.
rules.hint: Put a space at the end of each prompt.

rules.pass_text: You used a `while` loop so the chat can keep going
rules.fail_text: This needs a `while` loop
rules.correction: Write `while msg != "bye":` (or `while True:` and `break` on bye).
rules.hint: SETUP the message, CHECK for bye, CHANGE with input() inside the loop.

rules.pass_text: CHANGE: `input()` is inside the loop
rules.fail_text: `input()` for the next message must be inside the loop
rules.correction: Indent `msg = input("You: ")` under `while`.
rules.hint: If you only ask once, the loop cannot reach bye unless the first message already was bye.

rules.pass_text: You used `elif` for more than two replies
rules.fail_text: Use `if` / `elif` / `else` to pick a reply
rules.correction: One path for help, one for name, one for bye, and an else for everything else.
rules.hint: Python stops at the first true check, so handle bye on its own path.

rules.pass_text: The quit word is `bye`
rules.fail_text: Stop when the message is exactly `bye`
rules.correction: Compare to `"bye"` with `==` or `!=`. Spelling and spaces matter.
rules.hint: Type bye, all lowercase, with no extra spaces.

rules.pass_text: Your prompts have a trailing space
rules.fail_text: A prompt is missing a space at the end
rules.correction: Use `input("What's your name? ")` and `input("You: ")`.
rules.hint: Without that space, the answer sticks to the question.

tests.expected_stdout:
Hi Cole! Type bye to quit.
I heard: hello
Bye Cole!
includes: Hi Cole! Type bye to quit.
tests.pass_text: It greets Cole, replies to hello, then says Bye Cole!
tests.fail_text: The hello-then-bye path didn't match
tests.correction: We typed Cole, hello, bye. Print the greeting, I heard: hello, then Bye Cole! once at the end.
tests.hint: Handle bye inside the loop so the quit message prints, and stop after that.

fail_if_out_of_inputs.fail_text: The loop kept asking after we typed bye
fail_if_out_of_inputs.correction: The CHECK should become false (or you should break) when the message is bye.
fail_if_out_of_inputs.hint: Use `while msg != "bye":` and set msg from input() inside the loop.

tests.expected_stdout:
Hi Cole! Type bye to quit.
I know: help, name, bye
You are Cole
Bye Cole!
tests.pass_text: help, name, and bye each take the right path
tests.fail_text: A command printed the wrong reply
tests.correction: help → I know: help, name, bye. name → You are Cole. bye → Bye Cole!
tests.hint: Use elif for the extra commands, and keep bye on its own path.

mixed_review.title: Mixed review · after Lesson 4
mixed_review.intro: A short mix of Lessons 1–4. No new ideas. Guess first, then check.

questions.prompt: What does `print("name")` show on the screen?
questions.why: Quotes make a string, so Python prints exactly what's inside.

questions.prompt: What does `print(name)` show, if name stores Cole?
questions.why: No quotes, so Python looks up the variable.
Both are strings, so they join. That's concatenation, not math.

questions.prompt: `input("food")` plus the answer Chicken printed `foodChicken`. What was wrong?
options: The prompt was missing a space
Chicken should have been a number
questions.why: input() prints the prompt exactly as written. Put a space inside the quotes, before the closing quote.

questions.prompt: What type of value does `input()` always give you?
questions.why: Even if the person types 15, input() gives you the text '15'. Lesson 5 is about changing that.

mixed_review.title: Mixed review · after Lesson 8
mixed_review.intro: Lessons 1–8, with the bugs you've already met. Guess first, then check.

options: Leave it. Python will add them.
questions.why: str() turns the number into text so + can join it. Read a TypeError from the bottom.

questions.prompt: A TypeError appears. Where should you start reading?
options: From the bottom, at the last line
From the very first line only
Ignore it and run it again
questions.why: The last line names the error. That's the first place to look.

questions.prompt: `if password >= "python"` let zebra in. What should the check be?
questions.why: >= compares strings alphabetically, so zebra counted as true. == checks for an exact match.

questions.prompt: The grade checks started with `>= 70`, then `>= 90`. What grade did 95 get?
questions.why: Python stops at the first true condition. 95 is also >= 70, so it never reached the A check.

questions.prompt: A while loop asked for the password forever. What was missing?
options: CHANGE: input() was not inside the loop
SETUP: the variable was never created
A print after the loop, which is required
questions.why: The CHECK uses the password variable. If you never update it inside the loop, the CHECK stays the same forever.

questions.prompt: After a while loop ends, do you have to print something?
options: No. A final print is optional
Yes. Every loop must end with a print
Yes, or Python will show an error
questions.why: The loop is done when the CHECK is false. A print after the loop is only needed if you want to say something then.

mixed_review.title: Mixed review · after Lesson 12
mixed_review.intro: A mix of the whole Phase 0 toolkit, including lists, functions, dictionaries, and the chat.

questions.prompt: foods = ["chicken", "tacos", "pizza"]. What is `foods[0]`, and what is `len(foods)`?
questions.why: Counting starts at 0, so foods[0] is the first item. len counts items, not the last index.

questions.prompt: You write `def greet(name):` and the print line, but nothing appears. Why?
options: You defined the function but never called it
print does not work inside a function
questions.why: A def line only writes the recipe. You still have to call it, like greet("Cole").
You look up a dictionary by its label, not by a position number.

questions.prompt: The chat loop is `while msg != "bye":`, and msg starts as `""`. We type hello, then bye. How many times does `input()` inside the loop run?
questions.why: It asks once for hello, once for bye, then CHECK is false and the loop ends.

questions.prompt: In the chat, `help` is an elif after a check for `bye`. If the message is help, what prints?
questions.why: bye is false, so Python moves to the next check and matches help. It never reaches else.

questions.prompt: Why is `==` the right check for a password or for the word bye?
questions.why: == means is exactly this. >= compares order, which is how zebra got into the password program.
